messages.author: e7a185e1c89c24a2
messages.subject: barplot with secondary y axis
parts:
is there someone so kind in helping me to sort out this problem?
I want to create a barplot with a secondary y axis;
so far I've managed what follows but I can't figure how to properly
scale the third series here called "c" which is referring to the
secondary y axis
#-------------------------------------
a<-c(71,100)
b<-c(82,110)
c<-c(0.1,1.5)
par(mfrow=c(1,1), mai=c(1.0,1.0,1.0,1.0))
plot1<-barplot(rbind(a,b), beside=T, axes=T, names.arg=c("a","b"),
ylim=c(0,150), xlim=c(1,9), space=c(0,1), col=c("darkgray","white"),
yaxt="n")
plot2<-barplot(c, add=T, beside=T, names.arg="c",
col=c("darkgray","white"), ylim=c(0,2), space=c(0,7), width=1,
yaxt="n")
axis(side=2, at=seq(0,150,30), labels=seq(0,150,30))
axis(side=4, at=seq(0,2,0.2), labels=seq(0,2,0.2))
#-------------------------------------

but because I can't find a proper solution with the standard command
approach I'm wondering if there is (in fact there must be!) a solution
with ggplot...

any useful hint for that? just to steer in the right direction...

beside this I have a very humble proposal for this fantastic forum....
why not trying to construct a collaborative mind map of all wonderful
features of ggplot2 to be shared in a free space like http://www.mind42.com/?

thanks to all
max

hola luciano,

as far as I understand what you are pointing me is a link about the
problem of displaying "same converted
information for the same breaks" on two different axis;
instead, what I'm looking for is to have a double axis system dealing
with very much different range of variability;
in my given example the problem is that I need to "relax" the bindig
of the secondary y axis to the scale set for the first one (in oder to
have a proper scale setting: i.e not too much condensed); in fact, it
is something so trivial to do in almost all "spreadsheets" that I'm
quite surprised that this possibility is not (apparently) given in
R

max

messages.author: f7dbcab391554bfd
messages.subject: Re: barplot with secondary y axis
parts:
Luciano-

What you're trying to do (2, differently scaled axes) is not supported
in ggplot2 and is generally not considered a good idea, although it's
a popular question both here and elsewhere. I work with Brian, and
you're correct about what we're doing: 2 axes, where the axes are
simply transformations, such as miles to kilometers or pounds to
kilograms. That's still hard to do in ggplot2, but doesn't violate the
semantics of "Grammar of Graphics", which ggplot2 implements [ see
http://www.google.com/search?q=grammer+of+graphics ]

What you're asking to do breaks the underlying semantics and is widely
discourage for visualizations [ see http://tomhopper.wordpress.com/2010/08/30/graphing-highly-skewed-data/
and http://www.google.com/search?q=Stephen+Few+dual+scaled+axes ].

-Wil

messages.author: 439a20c9d67ff394
messages.subject: Re: barplot with secondary y axis
parts:
On Feb 17, 8:14 am, maxbre <ggplot2.max...@gmail.com> wrote:
> in fact, it
> is something so trivial to do in almost all "spreadsheets" that I'm
> quite surprised that this possibility is not (apparently) given in
> R

If I'm understanding you correctly, then luciano's reply seems
correct; ggplot literally will not do what you're looking for. The R
base graphics will certainly let you construct dual y axes (by hand,
essentially) if you like. The reason (to the best of my knowledge)
that this is not possible in ggplot is that dual y axes are generally
considered a very, very bad idea. They are often confusing and can be
made to say nearly anything you like.

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: barplot with secondary y axis
parts:
Hi:

Let me reinforce Joran's observation. Hadley is on record in the list archives saying that he doesn't support multiple axis scaling in ggplot2, a stance that I applaud. (I mean those situations where one wants to plot u vs. v and x vs. y in the same graphics region with the two [often unrelated] sets of scales populating opposite sides of their corresponding axis.) Excel lets you be as bad as you wanna be - OTOH, R's graphics systems make it difficult for you to perform bad graphics, but not impossible. That's a feature, not a bug. However, I do have some sympathy with those who would like to use related scales in different units (e.g., euros vs. USD, lb. vs. kg), as shown in one of the links referenced earlier in this thread.

Having said that, if you *really* want that double scaled plot, look to the twoord.plot() function in package plotrix, which works with the base graphics system.

Dennis
